title: CTE Units: ppm/°C vs ppm/°F vs 10⁻⁶/K
h1: Coefficient of thermal expansion units — ppm/°C, ppm/°F and 10⁻⁶/K
description: CTE is quoted as ppm/°C, µm/(m·°C) or 10⁻⁶/K — all numerically equal. But ppm/°F is 5/9 of the °C value. Confusing them cracks optical mounts and glass-to-metal seals.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: Steel's CTE is ~12 × 10⁻⁶/K. Invar's is 1.2 × 10⁻⁶/K — ten times lower. Precision optics need ppb-level control across a ±5 °C window.
body: Coefficient of thermal expansion controls how much a part grows per degree. The units mix SI and imperial degree sizes freely, and the ratio matters when you copy a spec from a European datasheet to a US drawing.
Invar 36: 1.2 ppm/°C. Fused silica: 0.55 ppm/°C. Borosilicate glass: 3.3 ppm/°C. Steel: 12 ppm/°C. Aluminium: 23 ppm/°C. Polycarbonate: 65 ppm/°C.

A 300 mm steel mount holding a Zerodur mirror (0.05 ppm/°C) contracts 3.6 µm across a 1 °C swing. Zerodur contracts 0.015 µm — a 240× mismatch that flexes the mirror surface out of λ/10 in a single night's temperature drop.
Multiply ppm/°F by 1.8 to get ppm/°C. Match materials by CTE, not by strength.

faqs.a: Yes — in/in/°F is a strain-per-degree ratio, dimensionally identical to ppm/°F.
Yes — datasheets quote average CTE over a stated range (often 20–100 °C). At cryogenic or high temperatures the value can shift by 30–50%.
